- `version: 3`. parseManifest accepts 3. ## 2. Selection state (pure, core)

`MusicSelection = { mode: "soundtrack" | "random"; soundtrackId: string | null; style: string | null }`.

- Style is fixed for the session. Default: the style of the first chosen soundtrack (the first soundtrack in manifest order that has tracks, unless a persisted choice is valid). The candidate set is always filtered by style.
- Mode `soundtrack` (default): selection for each scene considers only tracks of the current soundtrack, with the existing scoring (Bhattacharyya by default), hysteresis, dwell, min track time, hard cut and crossfade config. If the current soundtrack has no track whose hand-labeled `emotion` equals the scene's dominant emotion, fall back for that scene only to the best same-style track from any soundtrack with that emotion (then best same-style overall). This does not change the session soundtrack. The decision reports that it is a fallback so the player can say so.
- "Cambiar track" (existing Next): other tracks with the same dominant emotion inside the current soundtrack, cycling in score order, wrapping, skipping the current. If none, the same emotion in other same-style soundtracks. Then the existing fallback (next best overall within the style).
- "Cambiar banda sonora": moves the session to the next same-style soundtrack in stable manifest order, cycling, that has a track for the current scene's dominant emotion. It switches at once (user action, no dwell, no min-track rule) with `crossfadeSec` to that soundtrack's best match, sets the override like Next, and stays on that soundtrack for later scenes. Disabled (returns null) when no other soundtrack qualifies. If the scene is null (failed analysis), it moves to the next same-style soundtrack that has any track.
- "Aleatoria" toggle, mode `random`: on each scene change (when the scheduler would select), pick randomly among same-style tracks across all soundtracks whose emotion matches the scene's dominant emotion and whose score is within `randomTolerance` of the best such score (add `randomTolerance: 0.05` to MUSIC_CONFIG with a one-line why). The RNG is injected (`rng: () => number`, default Math.random in the app only) so tests are deterministic; core never calls Math.random by itself. Dwell and min-track rules still apply in random mode; the hysteresis margin does not (any eligible pick is fine), but keep the current track when it is itself eligible, so random mode does not churn on rescans.
- Toggling random off returns to `soundtrack` mode with the soundtrack of the currently playing track.
- Persist `{ mode, soundtrackId }` in localStorage (app side, one small helper, key like `lectoria.music.v1`). On load, ignore a persisted soundtrack id that is not in the manifest or not in the style. Guard against storage exceptions (private mode).

Integrate with core/music-schedule.ts with the smallest change that stays clean: e.g. the scheduler takes the selection and rng in its inputs, or a pure `candidatesFor(selection, manifest)` filter plus a soundtrack-aware ranking. Decide in the design and say why in one line. Keep all functions pure with explicit `nowSec`, no real timers in tests.

11|Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.

15|Take the first option that fully works:

17|1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.

73|## Lectoria rules
74|
75|- The text unit is the scene, not the paragraph or chapter.
76|- Paragraph ids are global, like `c12p34`.
77|- The emotion taxonomy has 8 ASCII ids: calma, alegria, tristeza, suspenso, misterio, aventura, combate, asombro. Jev returning `unknown` counts as low confidence and goes to the Muse override, which may return only the 8 ids. A hard failure stores no vector and the scene keeps the previous track. Never fake an emotion.
78|- Jev runs at `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with the model pinned to `jev-1.14.0`.
79|- Public-domain books only.
80|- Images follow the book text and the W. W. Denslow 1900 illustrations: silver shoes, nothing from the 1939 MGM film.

82|- Test with the cheapest models (Contributor). Use Standard for the final pass and the public chat.

84|## Product rules
85|
86|Owner decisions. Short and binding.
87|
88|- Desktop first. No mobile or iOS work now.
89|- The reader uses continuous scroll. The unit is the scene.
90|- A chapter holds several scenes. Each scene has its own emotion. Music changes at scene boundaries inside a chapter. No pagination.
91|- Reading position is the first paragraph visible at the top, tracked with IntersectionObserver.
92|- Paragraph ids carry a global ordinal `n`. Compare `n`, never id strings.
93|- `book.json` is frozen with a `textVersion` hash. Every cache key includes it.
94|- Scenes cover each chapter's paragraphs with no gaps and no overlaps. No scene crosses a chapter boundary.
95|- Emotions are distributions. Each scene stores the full Jev probability vector over the 8 ids, plus `intensity` (0 to 1) and `tempo` (energy, 0 to 1). The Muse override on low confidence edits the vector and records that it did. It never swaps in a single label.
96|- Music is about 15 tracks, pre-generated offline with MusicGen on Modal as one coherent soundtrack: same orchestra and instrumentation, same leitmotif style. Each track is a weighted blend of emotions and carries an emotion vector plus intensity and tempo. The proposed way to pick the blends: cluster the Oz scene vectors and use the centroids as track prompts.
97|- The player picks the track nearest to the scene vector, by cosine similarity over the vector plus intensity and tempo. Hysteresis stops it from flipping on small changes. Skip or change track overrides until the next scene.
98|- The owner listens to short clips before any full generation. Agents do not run Modal until the owner says so.
99|- MusicGen weights are CC-BY-NC. The hackathon demo is non-commercial. The generated tracks must say so in their README.
100|- Chat is low priority and simple. The context is the book text up to the reader's current position. The book prefix goes first and the question goes last, so readers share the prompt cache. Oz is about 55k tokens.
101|- The chat system prompt answers only from the provided text. It refuses knowledge beyond it, even if the model knows the book.
102|- A spoiler mode toggle is for readers who finished the book. It sends the whole text so they can ask about later events. No live Glimmer spoiler guard. No per-chapter summaries for chat. Citing passages is optional.
103|- Glimmer (open weights) keeps a pipeline role. Current decision: it writes the per-scene "why this music" explanation shown in the Developer View.
104|- Spikes come before feature code. Throwaway scripts in `scripts/spikes/` measure Muse Image (response format, latency, Denslow-style prompt), Meta `json_schema` structured output, and the Jev vector on a few Oz scenes. Results go to `docs/spikes.md`.
105|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars. Reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call and refund with `DECRBY` after. Reserve per call, including retries.
106|- The server clamps every model tool argument. Tool arguments are untrusted input.
107|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` (script and frame) and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` (images).
108|- The "Picture this" cache key is the paragraph range the selection touches (`firstPara..lastPara` ordinals) plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`. The prompt is built from those paragraphs.
109|- Images are cached only in Vercel Blob at deterministic paths (`addRandomSuffix: false`, check with `head()`). No Redis index. Routes return Blob URLs, never image bytes.
110|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Tokens live only in env.

112|## Security rules
113|
114|Summary. The full rules live in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
115|
116|- Secrets live only in env vars: `.env.local` locally (gitignored), Vercel env vars in prod.
117|- `.env.example` holds names only, never values.
118|- Never use a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable for a secret. Only public ids such as the Turnstile site key may use it.
119|- `core/` stays pure: no keys, no env reads, no network clients, no `server-only`. Key-holding clients live in `server/` (Next.js only, each file starts with `import 'server-only'`) and in `pipeline/` (Node scripts that read env). Callers inject them into `core` functions as arguments. Tests run `core` with fake clients.
120|- The pre-commit secret scan must pass. Never bypass it with `--no-verify`.
121|- Errors to the client are generic. Details go to server logs only, never with keys.
122|- Never log request headers.

124|## Writing rules
125|
126|Run docs, UI copy, and commit messages through the `unslop` skill: no filler, no hype, no emoji in headings, none of seamless, elevate, delve, robust, leverage. Headings use sentence case. Commit messages use an imperative subject under 72 chars, and the body says why.
127|
128|## Design
129|

45|
46|`Similarity = (scene, track, weights) => number`, where

1|# Contracts
2|
3|Music generation must never block the reader. Each module below owns one
4|job and can be swapped without touching the others. Import direction is
5|`core <- server` and `core <- app`. Server and client components never
6|import each other. `app/page.tsx` may import `server/books.ts`. Client
7|files never do.
8|
9|## Book data
10|
11|`data/books/oz/book.json` holds the frozen text: id, title, author,
12|`textVersion` hash, chapters with `start_n` and `end_n`, and paragraphs
13|with `id`, `ch`, `n`, and `text`. `analysis.json` is the scene source
14|the reader consumes: the same scenes plus Jev vectors, the Muse
15|override, and the `final` emotion. `scenes.json` is the pipeline
16|intermediate that `analysis.json` mirrors. The reader consumes the book
17|fields, scene ranges and titles, and the `final` vector with intensity
18|and tempo. It never sees `jev`, `muse_override`, or provenance.
19|`core/reader.ts` defines `buildReaderModel`, which joins paragraphs to
20|scenes by ordinal range and throws on unordered scenes or on paragraphs
21|covered zero or two times.
22|
23|## Music library
24|
25|The library is a static `public/music/manifest.json`, version 2, fetched
26|by the client from `/music/manifest.json`. A static file needs no route,
27|ships from the CDN, and swaps by replacing files only. Tracks may be
28|several minutes long and are not loops unless marked so.
29|
30|`MusicManifest = { version, tracks }`. `Track = { id, src, title,
31|emotion, vector, intensity, tempo, durationSec }` plus optional
32|`startSec` (default 0, where playback starts on first play and on each
33|loop), `loop` (default true), `source` (`generated`, `jamendo`, or
34|`recording`), `artist`, `composer`, `license`, `attribution`, and
35|`sourceUrl` (https only). `emotion` is the hand label: one of the 8
36|emotion ids in `core/types.ts`. The vector covers the 8 ids with finite
37|entries in 0..1. `core/music.ts` owns `parseManifest`, which rejects
38|unknown versions, missing fields, bad vectors, NaN entries, out-of-range
39|numbers, `startSec` outside its range, unknown `source` values, and any
40|`src` that is not a `/music/` path or `https` URL. The reader calls it on
41|every fetch, so a bad drop-in fails loudly in dev. Remote URLs need a
42|`media-src` addition in `next.config.ts`.
43|
44|## Similarity and config
45|
46|`Similarity = (scene, track, weights) => number`, where
47|`SceneSignal = { vector, intensity, tempo }`. The default is
48|`bhattacharyyaSimilarity`: both 8-emotion vectors renormalize to sum 1
49|(an all-zero vector gives an affinity of 0), `E` is the sum of
50|`sqrt(s_k * t_k)`, and the score is `weights.emotion * E` plus
51|`weights.intensity` and `weights.tempo` each for intensity and tempo
52|closeness. Scoring and ranking pass the resolved config weights in, so
53|a weights override changes the ranking. `cosineSimilarity` over
54|`buildFeatures` output stays as an exported alternative. One exported object,
55|`MUSIC_CONFIG`, holds `similarity`, `weights`, `switchMargin` (0.07),
56|`dwellSec` (20), `minTrackSec` (45), `hardCutMargin` (0.20),
57|`crossfadeSec` (3), and `hardCutCrossfadeSec` (1.5). Everything else
58|reads from it. Ranking ties go to the lower track id.
59|
60|## Selection scheduler
61|
62|`core/music-schedule.ts` is a pure state machine. The reader calls
63|`observeScene`, `tickScheduler`, `requestNext`, and `noteTrackEnded`
64|with explicit `nowSec` values, so all timing is testable without
65|timers. State holds the current track id and when it started, the active
66|scene id, the pending scene id and since when, and the skip override
67|with the scene it belongs to.
68|
69|A newly entered scene becomes pending and the dwell clock restarts, so
70|fast scrolling keeps only the newest scene. The first track ever plays
71|at once with no dwell. After the pending scene holds for `dwellSec` it
72|becomes active and the override clears. Then the best track switches in
73|only when it beats the current score by `switchMargin` and the current
74|track played `minTrackSec`, unless it wins by `hardCutMargin` (hard
75|cut, short fade). A second passes the active scene back through the
76|switch check, so a hold from `minTrackSec` releases on time, unless a
77|skip override stands: ticks return no change while it is set, and only
78|a new scene promotion clears it. A switch
79|reports its crossfade length: 3 s normally,
80|1.5 s for hard cuts. The skip choice holds until the next scene change;
81|after that, dwell and hysteresis apply with the override track as the
82|current track. A null scene means a failed analysis with no vector, so
83|it never triggers a switch. A non-looping track that ends fades into
84|the best remaining track, excluding the one that ended, and clears the
85|skip override.
86|
87|## Change track
88|
89|`nextTrack` cycles tracks hand-labeled with the scene dominant emotion
90|(argmax of the renormalized scene vector, ties by emotion order), ranked
91|by score with ties by lower id, wrapping around and skipping the current
92|track. When the current track has another emotion, it starts at the top
93|candidate. With no other same-emotion track it falls back to the best
94|track overall that is not current. A null scene cycles all tracks in id
95|order. One track or none gives null, and the UI disables the button.
96|
97|## Player
98|
99|`app/player.tsx` takes the track, the fade length for the latest switch,
100|the scene title, a skip flag, and callbacks. It owns two `audio`
101|elements, play state, volume, and the equal-power crossfade
102|(cos/sin gains over the fade time, driven by `requestAnimationFrame`).
103|It never uses the `loop` attribute. Volume lives in a ref, so the slider
104|never re-runs the track effect or touches `src`. A new track request
105|mid-fade cancels the pending fade and fades from the audible element to
106|the newest track. On load each track seeks to `startSec` once metadata
107|is available. Long tracks with `loop` true crossfade into the other
108|element playing the same track from `startSec` when `currentTime`
109|reaches `duration - fade`, where `fade` is the latest scheduler fade
110|length, or the config `crossfadeSec` when none was reported yet. When
111|`loop` is false the player reports the end and the scheduler picks the
112|next-best track excluding the ended one. Pause stops both elements and
113|freezes the fade in place; play resumes the audible elements from the
114|frozen point. Audio starts once, on the first press, with fade 0.
115|Audio starts only after the user presses play. Reduced motion is read in
116|state with a change listener and affects visuals only, never the fade.
117|
118|The bar shows Play/Pause, Volume, a Change track button (disabled when
119|Next has nothing to offer), the track title with its emotion label, and
120|attribution when present: composer or artist, license, and a source
121|link. On manifest failure the reader still renders and the bar shows a
122|short neutral note. UI motion stays under 200 ms. Controls are real
123|buttons and inputs with labels, visible focus, and keyboard use.
124|
125|## Image api
126|
127|Contract only, no routes. Request `{ bookId, textVersion, firstN, lastN
128|}` names the selection by touched paragraph ordinals. Response `{ url }`
129|is a Vercel Blob URL. The cache key is `firstN..lastN` plus
130|`textVersion` plus `promptVersion` at a deterministic Blob path with
131|`addRandomSuffix: false`. The server checks the path with `head()`
132|before generating and never returns bytes. The same paragraph range
133|reuses the image. Types live in `core/types.ts`.
134|
135|## Chat api
136|
137|Contract only, no routes. Request `{ bookId, textVersion, positionN,
138|spoilerMode, messages }` carries the chat history and the reader
139|position. The response is streamed text. The server builds context from
140|the book text up to `positionN`, or the whole book when `spoilerMode` is
141|on, with the book prefix first and the question last so readers share
142|the prompt cache. The system prompt answers only from that text and
143|refuses the rest. Types live in `core/types.ts`.
144|
145|## Quotas and budget
146|
147|Server only. Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with
148|Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after, one
149|reserve per call including retries. The server clamps every model tool
150|argument. Clients never see keys or raw errors. Generic messages go to
151|the client, details stay in server logs.

33|export interface Track {
34|  id: string; src: string; label: string;
35|  vector: Vector8; intensity: number; tempo: number;
36|  durationSec: number; loop: boolean;
37|}
38|export interface MusicManifest { version: number; tracks: Track[]; }
39|export function parseManifest(json: unknown): MusicManifest;
40|export function selectTrack(
41|  scene: { vector: Vector8; intensity: number; tempo: number } | null,
42|  manifest: MusicManifest,
43|  currentTrackId?: string | null,
44|  opts?: { margin?: number; exclude?: string[] },
45|): Track | null;

When `scene` is null it ranks on the current track first, which keeps playback stable through failed scenes.

55|Contract-only types live in `core/types.ts`, with no routes and no implementations:

64|
65|## Reader model shape
66|
67|New pure function in `core/reader.ts`:
68|
69|```ts
70|export interface ReaderParagraph { id: string; n: number; text: string; }
71|export interface ReaderScene {
72|  id: string; title: string;
73|  emotion: { vector: Vector8; intensity: number; tempo: number } | null;
74|  paragraphs: ReaderParagraph[];
75|}
76|export interface ReaderChapter { ch: number; title: string; scenes: ReaderScene[]; }
77|export interface ReaderModel {
78|  bookId: string; textVersion: string; title: string; author: string;
79|  chapters: ReaderChapter[];
80|}
81|export function buildReaderModel(
82|  book: Pick<Book, "id" | "title" | "author" | "chapters" | "paragraphs" | "textVersion">,
83|  analysis: { scenes: AnalyzedScene[] },
84|): ReaderModel;
85|```
86|
87|It joins paragraphs to scenes by `n` ranges in reading order, keeps `final` emotion or null for failed scenes, and drops analysis internals (`jev`, `muse_override`, provenance) so they never reach the client. It throws on unordered scenes or on paragraphs covered zero or two times, reusing the checks in `core/scenes.ts` where they fit.
88|
89|## Server side
90|
91|`server/books.ts` starts with `import 'server-only'` and exposes one function:
92|
93|```ts
94|export function loadOzBook(): { book: Book; scenes: AnalyzedScene[] };
95|```
96|
97|It reads `data/books/oz/book.json`, `scenes.json`, and `analysis.json` with a static import (build time, no request cost) and returns typed values. `app/page.tsx` calls it, runs `buildReaderModel`, and renders chapters, scene sections, and paragraphs as server HTML. Paragraph ids reuse `paragraphId` from `core/ids.ts`, which yields `c12p34` style ids. Choice: text renders on the server and only scene ids plus emotion triples pass as props to client components, so the full book text never duplicates in the client payload.
98|
99|## App side
100|
101|`app/page.tsx` owns layout: centered book column at the reading measure, quiet side panel with the "Chat comes later." placeholder, and the player bar slot. No chat code. Scene sections carry `data-scene-id` with a subtle divider and no other chrome.
102|
103|`app/reader.tsx` is the client container. It owns the manifest fetch (once, from `/music/manifest.json`, parsed with `parseManifest`), the active scene id, the current track id, and the skip override. On manifest failure the reader still renders and the bar shows a short neutral message. It passes the chosen track to the player.
104|
105|`app/player/` owns only playback: audio elements, play state, volume, and the skip button wired through an `onSkip` prop from the container.
106|
107|## Active scene tracking
108|
109|One `IntersectionObserver` watches scene sections. The reading line sits near the top third of the viewport, set with a `rootMargin` band around minus 30 percent. The active scene is the intersecting section whose top edge is nearest above the line. Choice: observer with a band instead of scroll math because jumps and fast scrolls then resolve in one callback with no position cache to maintain. Edge handling: short scenes still cross the band since sections span their paragraphs; when nothing intersects (fast fling between frames), keep the last active scene rather than guessing. On mount, compute from current scroll position so reloads mid book start on the right scene.
110|
111|## Player state machine
112|
113|States: `idle`, `playing`, `paused`, `crossfading`, `no music`. `idle` means no user gesture yet; `no music` means the manifest failed or is empty.
114|
115|```text
116|idle --press play--> playing (or crossfading when a track is already selected)
117|playing --track change--> crossfading --1.5s--> playing
118|playing --press pause--> paused --press play--> playing
119|any --manifest failure or empty--> no music
120|```
121|
122|Two `audio` elements fade against each other on change over about 1.5 s, then the old one pauses. `prefers-reduced-motion` sets the fade to 0. UI motion stays under 200 ms per tokens; the audio fade is not UI motion. Controls are real buttons with labels, visible focus, and full keyboard use. 123|
124|## Selection and skip override
125|
126|On each active scene change the container runs `selectTrack(sceneEmotion, manifest, currentId)` and stores the result as current. This matches the product rule that a skip holds until the next scene.
127|
128|## Placeholder manifest
129|
130|Choice: static `public/music/manifest.json` fetched by the client, because it needs no route, ships from the CDN, and a later swap replaces files only. `version: 1`, two tracks, `loop: true`, `durationSec: 10`:
131|
132|| Track | File | Label | Emotion source |
133||-------|------|-------|----------------|
134|| oz-test-01 | placeholder/oz-test-01-calma-t01.mp3 | Calm, flute and harp | cluster t01, intensity 0.229, tempo 0.245 |
135|| oz-test-02 | placeholder/oz-test-02-suspenso-t07.mp3 | Suspense, tremolo strings | cluster t07, intensity 0.530, tempo 0.539 |
136|
137|Vectors copy the t01 and t07 centroids rounded to 3 decimals; both already sum to 1.000 at that rounding, and the implementer renormalizes if any edit shifts the sum. `public/music/README.md` covers the swap (replace files and manifest, keep the shape, bump version) plus the CC-BY-NC note for MusicGen output in this non-commercial demo. 138|
139|## Test list
140|
141|Vitest, beside the code, no DOM library. `core/music.test.ts`: nearest by cosine wins; hysteresis keeps current within margin and switches beyond it; null scene keeps current and returns null without one; empty manifest returns null; `exclude` skips ids; ties follow manifest order; `nextAlternative` cycles all tracks and returns the single track to itself; `parseManifest` accepts the good manifest and rejects each bad shape. `core/reader.test.ts`: reading order, scenes ordered by `n`, every paragraph exactly once, null emotion for failed scenes, no `jev` or `muse_override` fields in output. 142|
143|## Risks
144|
145|Autoplay: browsers block sound before gesture, so the player must never call play on mount or on track change while `idle`; verify by loading and confirming silence until press. Observer: `find in page` and anchor jumps can set odd scroll positions, so the mount computation plus the keep-last fallback matter more than band tuning. 146|
147|## Fix pass
148|
149|Review findings 1 to 9 are fixed, 10 is now a motion state with a change
150|listener (visuals only, never the audio fade), and 11 went away with the

3|description: "Apply when writing stateful logic, or when code branches a lot or repeats a shape assumption across files."

6|
7|# Model the Domain
8|
9|Encode the real domain in a data structure instead of scattering it across conditionals. A structure that matches the domain makes invalid states unrepresentable and deletes branches. Choosing it at write time is cheap. Recovering it later reads as a refactor and gets deferred.
10|
11|Reach for:
12|
13|- A state machine instead of scattered booleans, phases, or lifecycle checks.
14|- A typed model instead of loose parameters or repeated shape assumptions.
15|- A map, registry, lookup table, or discriminated union instead of branching spread across files.
16|- A reducer or command/event model instead of ad hoc state mutations.
17|- A module organized around one body of domain knowledge instead of a sequence such as load, validate, transform, and save. Execution order is not ownership.
18|- A small module boundary that gathers repeated behavior, ownership, or invariants.
19|- A queue, cache, index, graph, tree, or normalized collection where the access pattern calls for it.
20|- Any other structure that fits. When none fits, work out what the code must never allow and how the data gets read, then find the structure that encodes exactly that.
21|
22|Do not force an abstraction. Prefer boring code if the current shape is already clear, local, and unlikely to grow. Be skeptical of an abstraction that adds indirection without removing branches, duplicated rules, invalid states, or lifecycle risk.
23|
24|The sign that you skipped this is a new feature that grows an existing if/else chain by one more branch, or a second boolean that must stay in sync with the first. Temporal decomposition is another sign. Phase-named modules repeat the same domain rules across steps.

8|# TypeScript best practices
9|
10|Apply the **type-system-discipline** principle skill first.
11|
12|| Rule | Summary |
13||------|---------|
14|| Discriminated unions | Model variants with a `kind` literal discriminant so impossible states can't be represented. No optional-field bags. |
15|| Branded types | Brand primitives with `& { readonly __brand: "X" }` so they can't be mixed up. Validate once at the boundary. A brand comes from a verifying type guard (`input is AgentId`), never from `as`. |
16|| Constructive modeling | Build the shape so the illegal value can't be constructed. `[T, ...T[]]` for non-empty, `[T, T][]` for even length, `start` plus `duration` for a range. Not a runtime guard, not a wish for refinement types. |
17|| Simplest total type | Keep `T[]` while every operation on it stays total. Strengthen to `NonEmpty<T>` only where the loose type forces `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. |
18|| `unknown` over `any` | External data is `unknown`. |
19|| Schemas before guards | Before hand-writing a property-by-property type guard, use the repository's runtime schema library and infer the type from the schema, such as `z.infer`. |
20|| No `as` casts | Every `as` is a runtime crash waiting. Cast only after validation. |
21|| Narrowing hierarchy | Discriminant switch > `in` operator > `typeof`/`instanceof` > user-defined type guard > `as`. |
22|| Type guards | Must verify the claim. A lying guard is worse than `as` because the bug hides behind a name that says it's safe. Name them `isX` or `hasX`. |
23|| Exhaustiveness | Inline `const _exhaustive: never = x;` in default arms so the compiler errors when a new variant is added. |
24|| `satisfies` over `as` | Validates the value without widening literal types. |
25|| Boundary validation | Parse where data crosses in, into a named domain type. `Record<string, unknown>` (however spelled) stops at that parse. Trust types inside. See the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. |
26|| Schema-derived types | Reach for `Pick`/`Omit`/`Parameters`/`ReturnType`/`Awaited`/`typeof` before declaring a new interface. |
27|| Object args | Pass objects, not positional, so argument order is self-documenting. Skip on hot paths (per-frame render, tokenizers, parsers). |
28|| Real tests | Don't mock what you can run. Prefer the framework's real test primitives with leak/disposable checks, and verify UI in a running build. Mock only what you can't run locally. |
29|| Structured telemetry | Prefer structured logger diagnostics with enough context to debug from an id. No `console.log` in shipped code. |
30|

7|# Foundational Thinking
8|
9|**Structural decisions** protect option value. **Code-level decisions** protect simplicity.
10|
11|**Data structures first.** Get the data shape right before writing logic. Define core types early, trace every access pattern, and choose structures that match the dominant paths.
12|
13|At code level, DRY the structure, not every line. Types and data models should converge. Three similar statements still beat a premature abstraction. Prefer explicit over clever. Test behavior and edge cases, not line counts.
14|
15|**Concurrency corollary.** Before sharing state between actors, ask "what happens if another actor modifies this concurrently?" If not "nothing", isolate.
16|
17|**Scaffold first.** If something helps every later phase, do it first. Ask "does every subsequent phase benefit from this existing?" CI, linting, test infrastructure, and shared types are scaffold. Sequence for option value: setup before features, tests before fixes. Keep commits small and single-purpose.
18|
19|Each increment should land a coherent abstraction or deepen one that exists. Do not spread a new capability across callers as special-case coordination.
20|
21|Subtraction comes before scaffolding. Remove dead code first, then lay foundations.

7|# Model the Domain
8|
9|Encode the real domain in a data structure instead of scattering it across conditionals. A structure that matches the domain makes invalid states unrepresentable and deletes branches. Choosing it at write time is cheap. Recovering it later reads as a refactor and gets deferred.
10|
11|Reach for:
12|
13|- A state machine instead of scattered booleans, phases, or lifecycle checks.
14|- A typed model instead of loose parameters or repeated shape assumptions.
15|- A map, registry, lookup table, or discriminated union instead of branching spread across files.
16|- A reducer or command/event model instead of ad hoc state mutations.
17|- A module organized around one body of domain knowledge instead of a sequence such as load, validate, transform, and save. Execution order is not ownership.
18|- A small module boundary that gathers repeated behavior, ownership, or invariants.
19|- A queue, cache, index, graph, tree, or normalized collection where the access pattern calls for it.
20|- Any other structure that fits. When none fits, work out what the code must never allow and how the data gets read, then find the structure that encodes exactly that.
21|
22|Do not force an abstraction. Prefer boring code if the current shape is already clear, local, and unlikely to grow. Be skeptical of an abstraction that adds indirection without removing branches, duplicated rules, invalid states, or lifecycle risk.
23|
24|The sign that you skipped this is a new feature that grows an existing if/else chain by one more branch, or a second boolean that must stay in sync with the first. Temporal decomposition is another sign. Phase-named modules repeat the same domain rules across steps.

8|# TypeScript best practices
9|
10|Apply the **type-system-discipline** principle skill first.
11|
12|| Rule | Summary |
13||------|---------|
14|| Discriminated unions | Model variants with a `kind` literal discriminant so impossible states can't be represented. No optional-field bags. |
15|| Branded types | Brand primitives with `& { readonly __brand: "X" }` so they can't be mixed up. Validate once at the boundary. A brand comes from a verifying type guard (`input is AgentId`), never from `as`. |
16|| Constructive modeling | Build the shape so the illegal value can't be constructed. `[T, ...T[]]` for non-empty, `[T, T][]` for even length, `start` plus `duration` for a range. Not a runtime guard, not a wish for refinement types. |
17|| Simplest total type | Keep `T[]` while every operation on it stays total. Strengthen to `NonEmpty<T>` only where the loose type forces `!`, a cast, or a "should never happen" throw. |
18|| `unknown` over `any` | External data is `unknown`. |
19|| Schemas before guards | Before hand-writing a property-by-property type guard, use the repository's runtime schema library and infer the type from the schema, such as `z.infer`. |
20|| No `as` casts | Every `as` is a runtime crash waiting. Cast only after validation. |
21|| Narrowing hierarchy | Discriminant switch > `in` operator > `typeof`/`instanceof` > user-defined type guard > `as`. |
22|| Type guards | Must verify the claim. A lying guard is worse than `as` because the bug hides behind a name that says it's safe. Name them `isX` or `hasX`. |
23|| Exhaustiveness | Inline `const _exhaustive: never = x;` in default arms so the compiler errors when a new variant is added. |
24|| `satisfies` over `as` | Validates the value without widening literal types. |
25|| Boundary validation | Parse where data crosses in, into a named domain type. `Record<string, unknown>` (however spelled) stops at that parse. Trust types inside. See the **boundary-discipline** principle skill. |
26|| Schema-derived types | Reach for `Pick`/`Omit`/`Parameters`/`ReturnType`/`Awaited`/`typeof` before declaring a new interface. |
27|| Object args | Pass objects, not positional, so argument order is self-documenting. Skip on hot paths (per-frame render, tokenizers, parsers). |
28|| Real tests | Don't mock what you can run. Prefer the framework's real test primitives with leak/disposable checks, and verify UI in a running build. Mock only what you can't run locally. |
29|| Structured telemetry | Prefer structured logger diagnostics with enough context to debug from an id. No `console.log` in shipped code. |
